newsitem.title: EGYPT: Mubarak defends controversial irrigation plan.
newsitem.headline: Mubarak defends controversial irrigation plan.

text.p: Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak dismissed on Friday criticism of his ambitious plans to irrigate the Western Desert with water from the Nile, saying some people would oppose development of any kind.
Mubarak, who is expected to inaugurate a canal into the desert next week, said Egypt had plenty of water to spare and had done the feasibility studies for the project 20 years ago.

The idea is to channel water from behind the Aswan High Dam into the desert, irrigate at least 500,000 acres (200,000 hectares) of land and relieve the population pressure on the Nile Valley, home to some 60 million people.

Opposition newspapers say the government has rushed into the project merely because the lake behind the High Dam lake is especially high this year and that it will end in expensive failure when the level of the lake goes down.
But Mubarak, speaking on state television, said all these criticisms were either baseless or misguided.

"We have groups who oppose absolutely any step forward. Whenever someone says something, we (Egyptians) have to come out and say 'No, no, no' -- (I mean) the forces that are against any development," he said.
"There is enough water...We still have a surplus of water. We will modernise the methods of agriculture in the old (Nile) valley and we are already recycling drainage water," he added.
"The studies were done 20 years ago and have been redone 100 times. No one can do better studies," he said.
He ridiculed critics who say that the project will collapse with a fall in the level of the lake, which is dependent on unpredictable rainfall in the Ethiopian highlands.
"We'll connect tunnels to the bottom of the lake and take out the water whether there is a Nile flood or not, whether the level goes up or not," he said.
But he also reassured Egyptians that the government could not spend billions of pounds (dollars) on the project quickly. "It's a project that will take us 20 years to finish," he said.

The government last week announced the first stage in an international tender to build what it says will be the world's biggest pumping station, to take 300 cubic metres (66,000 gallons) of water a second from the lake to the Toshka depression. The water will then flow north towards the New Valley, a string of oases in the Western desert.
